result: NREV12 provides a significantly better fit than GTR and NREV6 to most viral genome datasets across all genome types (dsDNA, dsRNA, ssDNA, ssRNA), as assessed by AIC and likelihood ratio tests. This finding was consistent across 107 of 141 datasets tested, with particularly strong support in ssRNA and ssDNA viruses as expected, but surprisingly also in dsDNA and dsRNA viruses.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly accept this finding, with one stating the authors 'provide solid evidence that...non time-reversible models may fit the real data better than the reversible substitution models commonly used in phylogenetics.' Another reviewer notes 'the results of the present study are not surprising' given previous work, indicating acceptance of the model fit findings. The editors describe this as 'solid evidence.'

result: Simulation studies show that as DNR increases, phylogenetic inference accuracy decreases for both GTR and NREV12 models. While NREV12 tends to yield more accurate trees than GTR when DNR>0, statistically significant improvements only occur at very high DNR values (>8) in lower diversity datasets—far exceeding the DNR values observed in empirical data (maximum 1.56).
evaluation: Reviewers accept the simulation findings, with one noting the authors 'show using simulated data that NREV12 leads to inferred trees that are closer to the true generating tree when the data incorporates a certain degree of non time-reversibility.' The editors confirm the authors provide 'solid evidence that it can be beneficial to include non-time-reversible models...when inferring phylogenetic trees out of simulated viral genome sequence data sets.'

result: The authors conclude that while non-reversible models are helpful for analyzing mutational processes, there is no pressing need for routine phylogenetic inference, though NREV12 may be prudent when DNR>0.5. They recommend case-by-case model assessment rather than routine adoption of non-reversible models.
evaluation: One reviewer explicitly challenges this conclusion, stating 'I miss an experiment that links the two findings to support the conclusion: in particular, an experiment that solves the following question: does the best-fit model also lead to better tree topologies?' This identifies a critical gap between demonstrating better model fit and demonstrating practical phylogenetic utility, leaving the practical recommendations uncertain.

result: Strand-specific substitution biases (as measured by DNR) are common across viral genome types, with most datasets showing DNR values between 0.0225-0.5. The distribution of DNR values does not cleanly differentiate which model provides the best fit, and substantial biases (DNR>0.25) occur irrespective of genome type.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the DNR characterization or the finding that strand-specific biases are common. The acceptance is implicit—reviewers focus their critiques on the implications rather than the measurements themselves. One reviewer notes the results are 'not surprising' given the biological context, indicating acceptance of the bias characterization.

result: The study analyzed 141 viral genome datasets (33 ssDNA, 30 dsDNA, 31 dsRNA, 47 ssRNA) using standard phylogenetic methods (MUSCLE alignment, RAxML trees, HyPhy model testing, AIC-c scores). Simulations used 5500 alignments evolved along scaled Avian Leukosis virus trees with varying DNR, assessed using weighted Robinson-Foulds distance.
evaluation: Reviewers do not question the methodological approach or dataset composition. The methods are standard and appropriately applied. The implicit acceptance through lack of critique, combined with the editors' assessment of 'solid evidence,' indicates the methods are sound and the data appropriate.
